en: Up to date with the latest news or developments; side by side
hook: A-BREAST: chest to chest, side by side, keeping pace.
story: Abreast. Every morning before class, Tahmid reads two newspapers, scans the business headlines, and listens to a news podcast on the bus. When the economics professor asked about yesterday's change in interest rates, only Tahmid knew the answer. He keeps abreast of current events: up to date with the latest news and developments. Literally, abreast means side by side, like soldiers marching shoulder to shoulder. Keeping abreast of the news means marching level with it, never falling behind. Synonym: up to date.

gre.s: Researchers in such a fast-moving field must read constantly to stay ____ of new findings; otherwise their own work can become obsolete within months.
gre.clue: otherwise their own work can become obsolete within months

en: To surprise or confuse someone, especially by contradicting expectations
hook: CONFOUND: CONFUSED and DUMBFOUNDED.
story: Confound. Everyone in the village said Ruksana could never pass the board exams: her family was poor, she had no tutor, and she studied by kerosene lamp. When the results came, she had the highest marks in the district. She confounded all their predictions: she surprised and confused people by contradicting what they expected. Confound can also mean to mix up, as in confounding two similar words. It comes from Latin for pouring together, everything mixed into confusion.

gre.s: The candidate's landslide victory managed to ____ the pollsters, who had confidently predicted for months that she would lose by a wide margin.
gre.clue: who had confidently predicted for months that she would lose by a wide margin

en: A temporary departure from the main subject
hook: DIGRESSION: DIGS off the main path.
story: Digression. Professor Latif began a lecture on the Mughal economy, then mentioned his trip to Agra, then the sweets he ate there, then his grandmother's cooking. Twenty minutes later he laughed and said, "Where was I? Ah yes, taxes." His students loved these digressions: temporary departures from the main subject. The verb is digress. Di means apart, and gress means step, as in progress: stepping aside from the path. Synonyms: tangent, aside, detour.

gre.s: Though the biography is generally tightly focused, its author indulges in an occasional ____, wandering away from her subject's life to discuss the history of the region.
gre.clue: wandering away from her subject's life

en: A difference or lack of agreement between things that should match
hook: DISCREPANCY: the numbers DISAGREE.
story: Discrepancy. At the end of the month, Tahsin checked the debating club's accounts. The receipts added up to forty-two thousand taka, but the bank held only thirty-eight thousand. Four thousand taka had vanished somewhere. She asked the treasurer to explain the discrepancy: a difference between things that should match. Auditors hunt for discrepancies between records, and lawyers for discrepancies between witnesses' stories. The word comes from Latin for sounding out of tune. Synonyms: inconsistency, mismatch, disparity.

gre.s: Investigators grew suspicious when they noticed a ____ between the company's public earnings reports and the figures it had submitted to tax authorities.
gre.clue: grew suspicious when they noticed

en: Deliberately deceptive; two-faced
hook: DUPLICITOUS: DUPLICATE faces, two-faced.
story: Duplicitous. Shafiq promised his business partner that their deal was safe and that he would never cheat him. That same evening, he met a rival company and secretly sold them his partner's customer list. To one man he showed a loyal face, and to the other a traitor's. He was duplicitous: deliberately deceptive, two-faced. Duplicity comes from Latin duplex, double, as in duplicate. A duplicitous person plays a double game. Synonyms: deceitful, treacherous, two-faced. Opposite: candid.

gre.s: The spy was so ____ that for years he convinced both governments of his loyalty while secretly betraying each to the other.
gre.clue: while secretly betraying each to the other

en: Convenient and practical, though possibly improper or immoral
hook: EXPEDIENT: the fast EXPRESS route, even if it cuts corners.
story: Expedient. The new bridge in Selim's town needed proper steel supports, but the contractor was behind schedule. Instead, he used cheaper rods and painted over the cracks so the minister could open it on time. It was expedient: convenient and practical in the moment, though improper. A year later it began to sag. As a noun, an expedient is a handy means to an end. Think: an expedient expedites things, often by cutting corners. Opposite: principled.

gre.s: Rather than address the root causes of the budget crisis, the council adopted the merely ____ measure of borrowing more money, which solved nothing in the long run.
gre.clue: which solved nothing in the long run

en: To invent something false in order to deceive; to construct
hook: FABRICATE: FABRIC of lies, stitched together.
story: Fabricate. Khalid missed the deadline for his research paper. To cover it up, he told his supervisor that his laptop had been stolen, invented a police report number, and even described the thief. None of it was true. He had fabricated the story: invented something false in order to deceive. Fabricate can also simply mean to construct, as in fabricating steel parts in a factory. On the GRE, it usually means to make up. Synonyms: concoct, invent, falsify.

gre.s: The journalist was dismissed after editors discovered that she had chosen to ____ several quotations, attributing to real officials words they had never spoken.
gre.clue: attributing to real officials words they had never spoken

en: Looking or feeling sad and gloomy
hook: GLUM: GLOOMY + DUMB-struck.
story: Glum. When Bangladesh lost a cricket match in the final over, a match they should have won, the whole tea stall went silent. Men stared into their cups. Nobody argued, nobody joked, and someone switched off the radio. Their faces were glum: sad and gloomy. Glum is a short, heavy word for a short, heavy mood. A glum expression, a glum forecast. Think of glum as gloom with the life squeezed out. Synonyms: morose, dejected, downcast. Opposite: cheerful.

gre.s: Despite the company's record profits, the shareholders' meeting was strangely ____, since everyone knew the beloved founder would announce his resignation.
gre.clue: since everyone knew the beloved founder would announce his resignation

en: A sign or person that announces something coming
hook: HARBINGER: a HERALD that announces what's coming.
story: Harbinger. In a Bangladeshi village, the first call of the koel bird after the cold weeks of winter makes grandmothers smile. Soon the mango trees will blossom and spring will arrive. The koel is a harbinger of spring: a sign that announces something coming. Harbingers can also be people, or omens of trouble: dark clouds are harbingers of a storm. Originally, a harbinger rode ahead of a king to arrange his lodging. Synonyms: herald, forerunner, omen, precursor.

gre.s: Many economists viewed the sudden collapse in housing prices as a ____ of the broader recession that would soon engulf the entire economy.
gre.clue: that would soon engulf the entire economy

en: Belonging naturally; essential
hook: INTRINSIC: from WITHIN (intra).
story: Intrinsic. Nabila solves maths puzzles at midnight with no exam coming, no prize, and no grade. Nobody asks her to; she simply loves the click of a proof falling into place. Her motivation is intrinsic: belonging naturally to her, essential, coming from within. Compare extrinsic motivation, like studying only for marks or money. Gold's colour and weight are intrinsic properties; its price is not. It comes from Latin intrinsecus, on the inside. Synonyms: inherent, innate, fundamental. Opposite: extrinsic.

gre.s: Her friends insisted that honesty was ____ to the founder's character, not a strategy adopted for appearances: even as a child she had refused to lie.
gre.clue: not a strategy adopted for appearances

en: Generosity in giving money or gifts
hook: LARGESSE: a LARGE gift.
story: Largesse. Every Eid, the descendants of an old landowning family in a Mymensingh village open their courtyard and hand out new clothes, rice, and money to hundreds of poor families. The line stretches down the road. Villagers have depended on this largesse for generations: generosity in giving money or gifts. Largesse is related to large: a large heart, a large purse. It often suggests a wealthy giver and grateful receivers. Synonyms: generosity, munificence, bounty. Opposite: stinginess.

gre.s: Although the museum's founder is now remembered chiefly for her ____, she was famously stingy in her early career, giving away nothing until her sixties.
gre.clue: she was famously stingy in her early career

en: A person who freely indulges in pleasures, ignoring moral restraints
hook: LIBERTINE: takes too many LIBERTIES with morality.
story: Libertine. In countless old Bengali films, the landlord's spoilt son wastes his inheritance on gambling, drinking, and parties that last until dawn. He laughs at his mother's warnings and mocks every rule the village holds sacred. He is a libertine: a person who freely indulges in pleasures, ignoring moral restraints. Libertine shares a root with liberty, but it means liberty with no self-control. Synonyms: rake, debauchee, hedonist, playboy. Opposites: puritan, ascetic.

gre.s: Unlike his brother, a notorious ____ who squandered his fortune on drink and gambling, the younger prince lived a life of strict self-discipline.
gre.clue: squandered his fortune on drink and gambling

en: Wrongdoing, especially by a public official
hook: MAL-FEASANCE: BAD doing (mal = bad).
story: Malfeasance. A district official was given money to build tube wells in fifty villages. Two years later, auditors found only ten wells, while the official had a new house and a new car. He was charged with malfeasance: wrongdoing, especially by a public official. Mal means bad, as in malpractice and malnutrition, and feasance means doing. Compare nonfeasance, failing to do one's duty at all. Synonyms: misconduct, corruption, wrongdoing. Opposite: probity.

gre.s: Once celebrated as a reformer, the mayor left office in disgrace after an inquiry uncovered years of ____, including bribery and the theft of public funds.
gre.clue: including bribery and the theft of public funds

en: Clearly evident (adj.); to show or display (verb)
hook: MANIFEST: so obvious it's in your hand (manus).
story: Manifest. For weeks, Rafi's grandfather insisted he was fine. But at the family dinner he could not lift his glass, and his speech was slurred. His illness was now manifest: clearly evident to everyone. As a verb, to manifest is to show or display, as in the disease manifested itself in his hands. A ship's manifest is a list of its cargo. The Latin root suggests something so plain you could grasp it by hand. Synonyms: obvious, evident, patent. Opposite: latent.

gre.s: Although the director insisted the project was on schedule, its failure was ____ to everyone else: half the buildings stood unfinished and the funds were gone.
gre.clue: half the buildings stood unfinished and the funds were gone

en: Extremely small; precise and detailed (pronounced my-NOOT)
hook: MINUTE (my-NOOT): as tiny as a MINI thing.
story: Minute. In a forensic lab, Doctor Joya examined a minute speck of blood on a shirt cuff, so tiny it was invisible to the naked eye. Her report described it with minute care, down to its exact position on a single thread. Pronounced my-noot, minute means extremely small, or precise and detailed. Do not confuse it with the minute on a clock. Minute, minuscule, and diminish share a root meaning small. Synonyms: tiny, infinitesimal, meticulous. Opposite: enormous.

gre.s: Although the changes to the manuscript appeared ____, they altered the meaning of several key passages in ways that scholars still debate.
gre.clue: they altered the meaning of several key passages

en: Fashionable; stylish
hook: MODISH: MODERN and in MODE (fashion).
story: Modish. Last winter, every young person in Dhanmondi seemed to wear the same oversized hoodie; this year it is handloom kurtas with white sneakers. Nabila's cousin Tisha follows each trend the moment it appears online. Her style is modish: fashionable and stylish. Modish comes from mode, as in a la mode, meaning in the current fashion. It can sound slightly mocking, hinting at a trend that will not last. Synonyms: fashionable, trendy, voguish. Opposites: outmoded, dowdy.

gre.s: The restaurant's décor, so ____ when it opened a decade ago, now looks hopelessly dated, a relic of a style no one wants anymore.
gre.clue: now looks hopelessly dated

en: Just beginning to exist; showing signs of future potential
hook: NASCENT: newly born (natal), like a newborn.
story: Nascent. A few years ago, two Dhaka students built a small app connecting passengers with motorbike riders. They had no office, only a shared laptop and big ideas. Ride-sharing in the city was nascent: just beginning to exist, but showing signs of future potential. Nascent shares a root with natal and renaissance, words about birth. A nascent democracy, a nascent talent, a nascent friendship. Synonyms: emerging, budding, embryonic, incipient. Opposite: mature.

gre.s: Investors hesitated to fund the ____ industry, since it was still in its infancy and no company had yet proved it could earn a profit.
gre.clue: still in its infancy

en: Lasting for a long time; recurring again and again
hook: PER-ENNIAL: through (per) the years (annus).
story: Perennial. Every monsoon, the same streets in Old Dhaka flood, rickshaws wade through knee-deep water, and the newspapers print the same photographs. Every year the city promises better drains. Waterlogging is a perennial problem: lasting a long time, recurring again and again. In gardening, perennial plants come back every year, unlike annuals. Think: per means through, and annus means year, so perennial means through the years. Synonyms: perpetual, enduring, chronic, recurrent. Opposite: ephemeral.

gre.s: Far from being a passing fad, the debate over free will is a ____ concern of philosophy, revived by every generation since antiquity.
gre.clue: revived by every generation since antiquity

en: Devoutly religious; sometimes, falsely or showily virtuous
hook: PIOUS: PRAYING faithfully.
story: Pious. Rahima Begum prays five times a day, fasts every Ramadan, and quietly sends money to an orphanage without telling anyone. Her neighbours consider her truly pious: devoutly religious. But pious has a second, sharper sense. When a corrupt businessman donates to a mosque only in front of cameras, people call it a pious show: falsely or showily virtuous. Synonyms for the first sense: devout, godly, reverent. For the second: sanctimonious, holier-than-thou. Opposite: irreverent.

gre.s: Voters grew weary of the senator's ____ sermons about honesty, especially once it emerged that he had lied repeatedly about his own finances.
gre.clue: once it emerged that he had lied repeatedly about his own finances

en: Occurring at a favorable time; lucky, as if by divine help
hook: PROVIDENTIAL: as if PROVIDENCE (God) sent it.
story: Providential. Anika's scholarship interview in Dhaka was at nine, and her bus broke down near Tangail at seven. She stood on the highway in despair. Then a car stopped: the driver was a professor heading to the very same university. She reached the hall with ten minutes to spare. The ride was providential: occurring at a favourable time, as if by divine help. Providence means divine care or guidance. Synonyms: fortunate, timely, opportune, heaven-sent. Opposite: ill-timed.

gre.s: The ____ arrival of a rescue ship, just hours before the leaking boat would have sunk, convinced the survivors that fate had intervened on their behalf.
gre.clue: just hours before the leaking boat would have sunk

en: Exceptional skill or ability
hook: PROWESS: a PRO's skill.
story: Prowess. When Babu first joined the village football team, nobody noticed him. Then, in the final against the neighbouring union, he dribbled past four defenders and scored from thirty metres. The crowd carried him on their shoulders, and everyone talked about his prowess: exceptional skill or ability. Prowess comes from an old French word for valiant, and first meant bravery in battle. Now it means any outstanding skill: athletic, academic, or technical. Synonyms: expertise, mastery, virtuosity. Opposite: ineptitude.

gre.s: Despite her undoubted ____ as a chess player, she lost the championship because she could not cope with the pressure of the final game.
gre.clue: Despite her undoubted

en: A split or division between groups, often over beliefs
hook: SCHISM (pronounced SIZ-um): a SCISSOR-cut through a group.
story: Schism. For decades, the village cricket club was united. Then a quarrel broke out over whether to accept sponsorship from a tobacco company. Half the members walked out and formed a rival club across the field, and some families stopped speaking to each other. The club suffered a schism: a split or division between groups, often over beliefs. The word is famous for religious splits, like the Great Schism between Eastern and Western Christianity. Synonyms: rift, rupture, breach. Opposite: union.

gre.s: What began as a minor disagreement over doctrine eventually produced a lasting ____ within the movement, as its followers divided into two hostile camps.
gre.clue: as its followers divided into two hostile camps

en: Making false spoken statements that damage someone's reputation
hook: SLANDER is SPOKEN; LIBEL is written.
story: Slander. After losing the student union election, Sabbir began telling everyone in the canteen that the winner had bought votes and cheated in exams. None of it was true, but the winner's reputation suffered. Sabbir was guilty of slander: making false spoken statements that damage someone's reputation. As a verb, to slander is to make such statements. Remember the difference: slander is spoken, while libel is written or published. Synonyms: defamation, calumny, smear. Opposite: praise.

gre.s: Unable to defeat his opponent on the issues, the candidate chose to ____ her instead, spreading false rumors that she had embezzled campaign funds.
gre.clue: spreading false rumors that she had embezzled campaign funds

en: Loyal, reliable, and hardworking
hook: STALWART: as STALL-WART, steady as a STALL that never moves.
story: Stalwart. For forty years, Rahim chacha has opened the village library every afternoon, through floods, strikes, and power cuts, without pay. When the roof leaked, he fixed it himself. When donations dried up, he kept going. He is a stalwart of the library: loyal, reliable, and hardworking. As an adjective, a stalwart supporter never wavers. Stalwart originally meant firmly built, like a strong pillar. Synonyms: steadfast, staunch, dependable. Opposite: fickle.

gre.s: A ____ supporter of the union for three decades, she never wavered, even when other members abandoned it during the long and bitter strike.
gre.clue: she never wavered

en: To ask or beg humbly
hook: SUPPLICATE: on your knees, SUPPLYING prayers.
story: Supplicate. When the river swallowed his family's land, an old farmer travelled to the district office. He waited for hours, then knelt before the officer with folded hands and begged for a small plot of government land to rebuild his home. He was supplicating: asking or begging humbly. The noun is supplication, and a person who does it is a supplicant. Think: sub means under, and plicare means fold, so you fold yourself low. Synonyms: beseech, implore, entreat. Opposite: demand.

gre.s: Defeated and desperate, the rebel leaders could only ____ the emperor, kneeling humbly before the very throne they had once vowed to destroy.
gre.clue: kneeling humbly before the very throne

en: Using few words; abrupt
hook: TERSE: TERSE is a terse word, just five letters.
story: Terse. Sara sent her boss a long, careful email asking for three days' leave for her sister's wedding, explaining every detail. The reply came in one word: "No." No greeting, no reason, no signature. It was terse: using very few words, abrupt. Terse can be efficient, like a terse summary, or rude, like a terse reply. Fittingly, terse is itself a terse word. Synonyms: curt, brusque, laconic, succinct. Opposites: verbose, prolix.

gre.s: Expecting a warm thank-you for her months of work, the volunteer was stung by the director's ____ reply, which consisted of a single, unsigned line.
gre.clue: which consisted of a single, unsigned line

en: A long, angry speech of criticism
hook: TIRADE: so long it TIRES everyone out.
story: Tirade. When the bus conductor overcharged him by ten taka, a passenger began shouting, and did not stop. For fifteen minutes he attacked the conductor, the bus company, the traffic police, and the state of the nation, while everyone stared out of the windows. It was a tirade: a long, angry speech of criticism. Think of a tirade as a tiring rant that never ends. Synonyms: diatribe, harangue, rant, broadside. Opposites: eulogy and panegyric, speeches of praise.

gre.s: Instead of offering constructive feedback, the critic launched into a furious ____ against the novel, denouncing its plot, its characters, and its author for nearly ten pages.
gre.clue: denouncing its plot, its characters, and its author for nearly ten pages

en: Relating to or done by everyone; applicable in all cases
hook: UNIVERSAL: across the whole UNIVERSE.
story: Universal. Over recent decades, Bangladesh worked hard to bring every child into primary school: boys and girls, rich and poor, city and village. Free textbooks, stipends for girls, and schools on remote river islands followed. The goal was universal education: done by or applying to everyone, with no exceptions. Think of the universe, everything there is. A universal truth holds in all cases; universal approval means everyone agrees. Synonyms: general, global, all-embracing. Opposite: particular.

gre.s: The proposal enjoyed nearly ____ support within the committee: of its forty members, only one voted against it.
gre.clue: only one voted against it

en: To defeat thoroughly
hook: VANQUISH: make the enemy VANISH.
story: Vanquish. In 1971, Bangladesh's freedom fighters, poorly armed and outnumbered at first, fought for nine months, until on the sixteenth of December the occupying army surrendered in Dhaka. The enemy had been vanquished: defeated thoroughly. Vanquish is stronger than defeat; it suggests total, final victory. You can also vanquish fears, doubts, or a disease. Picture the vanquished vanishing from the battlefield. Synonyms: conquer, overwhelm, rout, crush. Opposite: surrender.

gre.s: Although the champion had seemed invincible for a decade, the young challenger managed to ____ him in just three rounds, leaving no doubt about who was superior.
gre.clue: leaving no doubt about who was superior

en: Full of sorrow; very bad or deplorable
hook: WOEFUL: full of WOE.
story: Woeful. The new government hospital in Rakib's district looked impressive from outside. Inside, there were two doctors for three hundred patients, no working X-ray machine, and medicines stored in cardboard boxes on the floor. A journalist described the conditions as woeful: very bad, deplorable. Woeful also means full of sorrow, as in a woeful song or a woeful face. Woe is grief, and woeful is full of it. Synonyms: deplorable, lamentable, dismal. Opposite: excellent.

gre.s: Although the school boasted of its modern facilities, inspectors found its science laboratories in ____ condition, with broken equipment and no working gas supply.
gre.clue: with broken equipment and no working gas supply
